title: Broken access control
brief: 16:55. A customer reports seeing another company's order in the portal. The order page takes the number straight from the address.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The page only checked that you were signed in, not whose order it is.
teaches: Authentication is not authorisation: check the owner on every request, on the server
Deny by default, in one place every route goes through
Unguessable ids and hidden links are obscurity, not access control

value.title: Customer portal: orders

fix.prompt: Pick every change that makes the server check ownership, and any that makes sure it is checked every time.

options.label: Scope the query to the signed in customer
code: - const order = await db.one('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);
+ const order = await db.oneOrNone('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id]);
options.why: The server only ever returns an order that belongs to the person asking. Return not found for everyone else.

options.label: Deny by default: one shared authorise() that every route must pass
options.why: Access control that depends on each developer remembering will be forgotten somewhere. A shared default fails closed.

options.label: Use random UUIDs instead of counting order numbers
options.why: Harder to guess, but anyone who ever sees one (a shared link, an email, a log) can still read that order. That is obscurity, not access control.

options.label: Only show links to your own orders in the interface
options.why: The attacker types the address. The interface does not enforce anything.

options.label: Log every order page view
options.why: Useful for spotting abuse afterwards, but it does not stop it.

setup.title: Workbench
setup.body: Review the order page access bug

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The page only checked that you were signed in, not whose order it is.

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The page checked that you were signed in, and never asked whose order it was. Changing 1002 to 1003 showed another customer's address and phone number, and counting upwards showed all of them.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: One number, someone else's data
body: The page checked that you were signed in, and never asked whose order it was. Changing 1002 to 1003 showed another customer's address and phone number, and counting upwards showed all of them.
This is the number one web risk for a reason: it is easy to write and hard to see in a demo.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: The query itself now includes the owner, so another customer's order simply is not found. And a shared default deny means a new route that forgets access control fails closed instead of open.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: The server decides, every time
body: The query itself now includes the owner, so another customer's order simply is not found. And a shared default deny means a new route that forgets access control fails closed instead of open.
Check on the server, on every request, in one place.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Random ids and hidden links make the attack harder to stumble on. They do not make it forbidden: the moment one id leaks, anyone holding it can read that order, because the server still never checks.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Hard to guess is not the same as forbidden
body: Random ids and hidden links make the attack harder to stumble on. They do not make it forbidden: the moment one id leaks, anyone holding it can read that order, because the server still never checks.
The check belongs on the server, against the signed in user.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
